draft.title: Erasure and evaluation
card: Late in the reign of Thutmose III, many images and names of Hatshepsut were chiselled out or hacked down at sites such as Deir el-Bahri. Some statues were smashed and buried.
Historians disagree about why. Some argue it was personal anger. Others argue it was meant to protect the line of kings who followed, so that no later claim could be built on a female ruler.
The timing matters. The damage came late in his reign, about twenty years after she died, so it is hard to explain as an act of immediate revenge.
Judging her reign means weighing evidence. Her building and the Punt expedition suggest a successful rule, but the erasure shows that later rulers did not all honour her.
draft.remember: The erasure came late, its cause is debated, and a fair judgement of her reign weighs all the evidence.

a.q: Why do some historians doubt that the erasure was an act of immediate revenge by Thutmose III?
opts: It began late in his reign, long after she had died
It only damaged her statues and left her temples alone
It was carried out by priests of Amun, not by the king
It also removed the names of kings who ruled before her
a.why: The damage came late in his reign, about twenty years after her death, so a sudden burst of anger is a weak explanation. The claim that her temples were untouched is wrong, because images at Deir el-Bahri were damaged.
a.clue: Think about when the damage happened.

b.q: A student says the erasure proves Hatshepsut's reign was a failure. What is the best reply from a historian's point of view?
opts: It shows later attitudes, but her reign needs all the evidence
It shows all Egyptians hated her, so her building is irrelevant
It shows she was a true king, as only kings were ever erased
It is useless as evidence, because it destroyed the sources
b.why: The erasure is evidence of later attitudes, and its cause is still debated. It has to be weighed with her building and the Punt expedition. Treating it as proof of failure uses one piece of evidence and ignores the rest.
b.clue: A fair judgement uses more than one source.
